## Mexico City, Mérida and the Maya cities: how the six-day tour works

Over **6 days and 5 nights**, you discover two very different historical regions of Mexico. In the capital, the focus is on the legacy of ancient Tenochtitlan, colonial architecture, the National Museum of Anthropology and [Teotihuacan](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/). On the Yucatán Peninsula, the itinerary continues through [Mérida](/mexico/place/merida/), [Uxmal](/mexico/place/uxmal/), [Kabah](/mexico/place/kabah/) and [Chichén Itzá](/mexico/place/chichen-itza/).

This sightseeing trip is designed for travelers with limited time who still want to experience several cultural eras. Its key difference from the overland route through Calakmul and Palenque is the **flight between Mexico City and Mérida**, which requires you to purchase a ticket separately and coordinate the timing.

## Two sightseeing days in the capital and Teotihuacan

In [Mexico City](/mexico/place/mexico-city-and-teotihuacan/), you visit the historic center, including the Zócalo, the Metropolitan Cathedral and monuments from different periods. An important museum stop is the National Museum of Anthropology, whose collections explore the country's pre-Hispanic cultures.

The following day includes [Teotihuacan](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/): the Avenue of the Dead, the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon, the Temple of the Feathered Serpent and other structures of the ancient city. A visit to the Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe, an important Catholic pilgrimage site, is also planned.

This part of the journey provides context for the Yucatán monuments: you first encounter the cultures of central Mexico, then explore Maya cities that developed in a different region and natural environment. Comfortable closed-toe shoes, water and sun protection are essential for the archaeological walks.

## Mexico City–Mérida flight: what matters most

**The domestic flight ticket is not included in the tour price.** Day four involves a transfer to Mexico City airport, the flight to Mérida, a meeting on arrival and a city sightseeing tour. To take part in that tour, **you must land in Mérida before 1:00 p.m.** Any other arrival time should be agreed in advance.

Do not overlook this requirement when booking flights independently. Allow time for leaving your hotel, checking in for the domestic flight, collecting baggage and traveling from the airport. A late arrival could shorten the sightseeing tour or make it impossible to run that day.

In [Mérida](/mexico/place/merida/), the itinerary covers the cathedral, Casa de los Montejo, the Government Palace and Paseo de Montejo. However, entering the interior of Casa de los Montejo as a museum visit is **not separately included**. Listing a landmark in the itinerary does not automatically mean that admission to every interior space is covered.

## Uxmal and Kabah: Puuc architecture in one day

Day five is dedicated to two archaeological sites south of Mérida. [Uxmal](/mexico/place/uxmal/) is famous for the Pyramid of the Magician, the Governor's Palace and its intricately decorated buildings. Puuc architecture is especially well represented here: ornamental facades and stone masks distinguish the region from many other Maya cities.

Nearby [Kabah](/mexico/place/kabah/) complements this visit. Its celebrated Temple of the Masks is adorned with numerous representations of the rain god Chaac. Exploring both complexes on the same day reveals the similarities of the regional style and the differences between the individual architectural ensembles.

Group transportation, admission tickets and a local English- and Spanish-speaking guide are included. After returning to Mérida, the evening is free. Whether to take an independent walk or choose a restaurant is up to you.

## Chichén Itzá and the transfer to Cancún

The final day features [Chichén Itzá](/mexico/place/chichen-itza/), an archaeological complex containing the Temple of Kukulcán, the Great Ball Court, colonnades and the Sacred Cenote. The route then ends with a transfer to [Cancún](/mexico/place/cancun/).

Lunch on this day is **not included**. Drop-off in the Riviera Maya or Tulum area carries an additional transfer charge of **$30 per person**. This is an optional final-transfer arrangement, not accommodation on the coast included in the package.

If you plan to extend the journey with a beach holiday, arrange the nights after the sightseeing itinerary in advance. None of these six days includes a free day at the beach.

## Accommodation, guides and expenses

The price includes **5 nights in standard rooms** at the specified hotels or comparable properties, breakfasts, one lunch, group transfers and excursions, admission to the listed attractions and hotel taxes. English-speaking assistance is included in the standard option; excursions also use English- and Spanish-speaking guides. **A Russian-speaking guide is available for an additional charge.**

International and domestic flights, including **Mexico City–Mérida**, are not included. Meals and services outside the itinerary, personal expenses, tips and additional transfer options are also paid separately. These are important distinctions when comparing the prices of two trips of the same duration.

If you want to visit several Maya archaeological regions, including forest sites, compare this itinerary with the [Cancún–Tulum–Calakmul–Palenque–Uxmal–Chichén Itzá tour](/mexico/tour/mexico-cancun-tulum-palenque-uxmal-chichen-itza/). If you would rather add free days on the Pacific coast, the [Triangle of the Sun](/mexico/tour/mexico-triangle-of-the-sun/) is another option.

## Who this itinerary suits

This program is for travelers who enjoy full museum and archaeological days but prefer to connect distant regions by domestic flight. Flying saves days of overland travel, although it requires careful coordination and additional spending.

The most important step before choosing this tour is to **check the Mexico City–Mérida flight first and make sure it arrives before 1:00 p.m.** Then consider your budget, preferred guide language and the drop-off arrangements in Cancún. Other options can be found in the [Mexico tours catalog](/mexico/tour/).

## Frequently asked questions about the Mexico City–Yucatán route

### Is the Mexico City–Mérida flight included?

No. The flight is paid for separately, and its schedule needs to be coordinated with the sightseeing program on day four.

### Why must I arrive in Mérida before 1:00 p.m.?

Because a guided sightseeing tour of Mérida is scheduled after your arrival and transfer that same day. A later flight may disrupt the day's itinerary.

### Can I book a Russian-speaking guide?

Yes, Russian-speaking assistance can be booked **for an additional fee**. The standard program includes English-speaking assistance and local English- and Spanish-speaking guides.

### What is the difference between Uxmal and Kabah?

Both cities belong to the Puuc architectural tradition. [Uxmal](/mexico/place/uxmal/) is known for its large architectural ensembles and the Pyramid of the Magician, while [Kabah](/mexico/place/kabah/) is known, among other features, for the Temple of the Masks and its carved decoration.

### Does the tour include a beach holiday in Cancún?

After visiting Chichén Itzá, the program concludes with a transfer to Cancún. Extra nights at the beach must be booked separately, and drop-off in Riviera Maya or Tulum costs an additional $30 per person.

## Mexico's Colonial Treasures: Querétaro, San Miguel, Guanajuato and Guadalajara

[Mexico's Colonial Treasures](/mexico/tour/mexico-city-queretaro-colonial-treasures/) is a **four-day route with three overnight stays**, beginning in Mexico City and ending in Guadalajara. It passes through historic centers associated with colonial-era architecture, the independence movement and Mexican art.

This format suits travelers who want to see several distinct cities of central Mexico in one short trip. The defining feature is the steady journey westward: you do not return to Mexico City every evening, and the overnight location changes almost every day.

## Day-by-day route: from Mexico City to Guadalajara

| Day | Main stops |
| --- | --- |
| 1 | Mexico City – Querétaro – San Miguel de Allende |
| 2 | San Miguel – Dolores Hidalgo – Guanajuato |
| 3 | Guanajuato – Guadalajara |
| 4 | Breakfast and departure flight from Guadalajara |

Each journey adds a new chapter to the preceding city. Querétaro is noted for its Baroque architecture, San Miguel for its picturesque center and artistic community, Dolores Hidalgo for the beginning of the independence struggle, Guanajuato for its narrow lanes and theaters, and Guadalajara for its major museums and murals.

## Day 1: Querétaro and San Miguel de Allende

Travelers leave Mexico City for [Querétaro](/mexico/place/queretaro/). Its historic district preserves a combination of a regular colonial street plan and winding lanes in older neighborhoods. UNESCO recognizes the city's wealth of civil and religious architecture from the 17th and 18th centuries.

The tour includes the arches of the city's monumental aqueduct, Casa de la Corregidora and the Church of Santa Rosa de Viterbo. These buildings reveal different aspects of urban life: water supply, civic administration and religious architecture.

After the walk, the journey continues to [San Miguel de Allende](/mexico/place/san-miguel-de-allende/). The striking facade of the Parroquia de San Miguel Arcángel dominates the center, surrounded by squares, cafés, artists' workshops and galleries. The city is known for its warm-toned houses and cobbled streets, which are particularly pleasant for an evening stroll. The first overnight stay is here.

## Day 2: Dolores Hidalgo and Guanajuato

After breakfast, the group travels to [Dolores Hidalgo](/mexico/place/dolores-hidalgo/). This city has a prominent place in Mexican history: in 1810, Miguel Hidalgo called for an uprising against Spanish rule here. The sightseeing program focuses on colonial streets, artisan shops and local traditions.

Next comes [Guanajuato](/mexico/place/guanajuato/), a very different-looking city. Colorful houses climb the hillsides, roads disappear into tunnels, and the old center is made up of narrow streets and small squares. Scheduled stops include the Alley of the Kiss, Juárez Theater, the Basilica of Our Lady of Guanajuato and Plaza de la Paz.

For architecture enthusiasts, this is one of the most varied days: sites associated with national independence in the morning, followed by a city of theaters, mountain slopes and colonial facades toward evening. The group spends the night in Guanajuato after the tour.

## Day 3: Guadalajara, murals and a major city market

The itinerary continues to [Guadalajara](/mexico/place/guadalajara/). Your introduction begins in its historic center, with the cathedral and Plaza de Armas. Hospicio Cabañas deserves particular attention: this UNESCO World Heritage complex is famous for monumental murals by the artist José Clemente Orozco.

The itinerary also includes San Juan de Dios Market. After museums and churches, it offers a completely different experience: market stalls, handicrafts, regional food and everyday city life. The third night is spent in Guadalajara, followed by an airport transfer after breakfast the next morning.

## Why the route takes exactly four days

The program's advantage is the opportunity to visit several historically significant cities in a short period. There is a trade-off, however: drives separate the walking tours, and not every city has a free day of its own. Those who want to explore San Miguel's art galleries in depth or stay several nights in Guanajuato may prefer a longer, custom-designed journey.

A particularly convenient feature is that the route has **different starting and finishing points**. When choosing flights, plan for Mexico City as your arrival point and Guadalajara as your departure point, rather than automatically booking a return flight from Mexico City.

## Accommodation, excursions and expenses

Ada Tours includes three nights in standard rooms at the named or comparable hotels, American-style breakfasts on days two through four, private transfers and excursions with an English-speaking guide, the specified admission tickets and hotel taxes. Ground transportation also has a baggage limit: one suitcase and one small piece of hand luggage per person.

The tour costs **from $1010**; the short price description does not specify the basis on which this amount is calculated. Consult the detailed offer conditions to establish the price for your particular group size. International flights, air taxes, lunches, dinners, personal expenses and tips for the driver and guide are not included.

## How this trip differs from other Mexico tours

The [Day of the Dead in Mexico program](/mexico/tour/mexico-day-of-the-dead/) has a different purpose: it is tied to late October and includes family remembrances, Mixquic and Huaquechula. The [Southern Adventure](/mexico/tour/southern-mexico-short-adventure/) travels through Chiapas and Yucatán to Maya archaeological sites.

Choose the four-day Colonial Treasures tour if you want to concentrate on the historic cities of central Mexico, galleries, architecture and the story of independence. The [full Mexico tours catalog](/mexico/tour/) lets you compare destinations by duration and included attractions.

## Frequently asked questions about the colonial route

### How many days are needed for Querétaro, San Miguel and Guanajuato?

This itinerary allocates **4 days and 3 nights** to these cities together with Dolores Hidalgo and Guadalajara. It is designed around journeys between cities and introductory sightseeing, not long stays in one location.

### Where does the tour start and finish?

It starts in Mexico City and ends in Guadalajara, with an airport transfer on day four.

### Is a private guide included?

Yes. Private excursions and transfers with an English-speaking guide are included.

### Can I visit Teotihuacan within these four days?

Although this tour starts in Mexico City, its listed stops **do not include a separate sightseeing day at Teotihuacan**. Do not assume it is included simply because the site is near the city where the journey begins.

## Day of the Dead in Mexico: 9 days from Mexico City to nighttime Mixquic

Día de los Muertos is Mexico's annual celebration honoring the dead, held in late October and the first days of November. Families set up altars with photographs, candles, flowers and offerings of food, visit cemeteries and gather with loved ones. This tradition is inscribed on UNESCO's list of intangible cultural heritage. It is observed differently from place to place, from home altars in a small town to nighttime cemetery visits in a crowded district of the capital.

[Ada Tours' Day of the Dead in Mexico tour](/mexico/tour/mexico-day-of-the-dead/) lasts **9 days and 8 nights**. The itinerary is designed so that you visit [Puebla](/mexico/place/puebla/), [Huaquechula](/mexico/place/huaquechula/) and [Mixquic](/mexico/place/mixquic/) during the celebrations themselves. Along the way, travelers discover Mexico City's art, [Teotihuacan](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/), Cholula and the canals of [Xochimilco](/mexico/place/xochimilco/).

## Why the dates matter for this journey

The itinerary is tied to the holiday calendar. It starts in Mexico City on **October 27**, visits Huaquechula on **October 31**, and reaches Mixquic for the evening of **November 1**. Two full sightseeing days follow before departure on November 4. The year of a particular departure and available places must be confirmed separately: annual departures on these dates are not guaranteed.

A conventional route through Mexico's historic cities can be taken in different seasons. The Day of the Dead requires a different approach: a particular evening in a particular community matters. Move the trip by a week and the pyramids and museums will still be there, but the family commemorations and festive decorations will be quite different.

| Itinerary dates | Main experience |
| --- | --- |
| October 27–30 | Mexico City, art, Teotihuacan, Puebla |
| October 31 | Cholula and the altars of Huaquechula |
| November 1 | Atlixco and evening in Mixquic |
| November 2–4 | Xochimilco, museums, departure |

## The first days: from urban history to folk traditions

Following arrival and check-in in Mexico City, the itinerary introduces the capital's historic center: the Plaza of the Three Cultures, Zócalo, cathedral and Palace of Fine Arts. Another day focuses on Coyoacán and two art destinations: Frida Kahlo's Blue House and the Anahuacalli Museum, created by Diego Rivera to house a collection of ancient Mexican art.

On day four, the route passes the Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe and archaeological [Teotihuacan](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/), home to the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon. The travelers then continue to [Puebla](/mexico/place/puebla/) and learn about local cemetery traditions. In this way, the holiday gradually enters the itinerary against the backdrop of central Mexico's historic landmarks.

## October 31: Cholula and the family altars of Huaquechula

The next day, the group sets out for [Cholula](/mexico/place/cholula/), known for its great pre-Hispanic pyramid and architecture at the foot of the volcanoes. The next stop is [Huaquechula](/mexico/place/huaquechula/), a small town where household altars have a particularly important place in the local Day of the Dead tradition. They are adorned with flowers, candles, photographs and food in memory of loved ones.

This visit offers an opportunity to see how the holiday is observed beyond the large urban parades. The emphasis here is on family remembrance and the preparation of homes, rather than a staged performance. Visits should be respectful: altars may be in private spaces, and permission to photograph them should be requested locally.

The same day includes a return to Puebla and a tour of its historic center, cathedral and richly decorated Chapel of the Rosary.

## November 1: Atlixco and nighttime Mixquic

The day starts in [Atlixco](/mexico/place/atlixco/), a city of flowers where floral decorations and historic neighborhoods play an important role. The group then heads back toward Mexico City to spend the evening in [Mixquic](/mexico/place/mixquic/).

This evening is one of the main reasons to choose the itinerary. In Mixquic, families decorate graves with flowers and candles, bring offerings and spend time beside the resting places of relatives. Candlelight and decorated streets create a recognizable festive scene, but the meaning of the occasion remains deeply personal.

It is a long sightseeing day: Atlixco in the morning, followed by a drive and an evening program. Before traveling, ask Ada Tours about the approximate length of the stop, the order of the cemetery visit and photography restrictions.

## What happens on the remaining days

November 2 includes walks through San Ángel, a visit to the University City campus and a boat excursion along the canals of [Xochimilco](/mexico/place/xochimilco/). On November 3, the itinerary features Chapultepec, the National Museum of Anthropology and an evening lucha libre show. On November 4, an airport transfer follows breakfast.

The journey thus brings together several sides of Mexico: family rituals, ancient cultures, modern art and urban traditions. Museum visits come after the principal festive events, when the itinerary no longer needs to center on a specific holiday date.

## Accommodation and price

The package includes 8 nights in standard rooms at the stated hotels or comparable properties, breakfasts from day 2 through day 9, private transfers and excursions with an English-speaking guide, specified admission tickets and hotel taxes.

**The price starts at $2015 per person for a group of 6, sharing a DBL room.** This is the stated basis for the quote and cannot simply be applied to a trip for two or to single occupancy. International flights, airport taxes, lunches, dinners, personal expenses and tips are paid separately. Specific visa requirements depend on citizenship.

## Who will enjoy this tour

The itinerary is designed for travelers drawn by the Día de los Muertos tradition itself and comfortable with busy sightseeing days. It is also appealing to enthusiasts of history and Mexican art: [Teotihuacan](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/), Coyoacán and the National Museum of Anthropology complement the celebrations.

If your main interest is architecture and historic cities without fixed holiday dates, consider [Mexico's Colonial Treasures](/mexico/tour/mexico-city-queretaro-colonial-treasures/). For a longer exploration of Chiapas's landscapes and Maya archaeological sites, try the [Southern Adventure](/mexico/tour/southern-mexico-short-adventure/). All options appear in the [Mexico tours catalog](/mexico/tour/).

## Frequently asked questions about the Day of the Dead tour

### When do the main holiday activities take place on this route?

The visit to Huaquechula takes place on October 31, and the evening trip to Mixquic on November 1. Other excursions occupy the dates from October 27 through November 4.

### Can I take the same itinerary in summer?

The cities and monuments can be visited in other seasons, but **the holiday experiences depend on late October and early November**. A summer trip to these places would be a different travel product.

### What expenses does the $2015 cover?

The starting price of $2015 is per person in a group of six, based on double occupancy. The package includes eight hotel nights, breakfasts, private excursions, transfers and admission tickets under the stated tour conditions. Air tickets and certain additional expenses are paid separately.

### May I photograph family altars and cemeteries?

Local rules apply in public places, while family altars and burial sites deserve particular respect. Ask your guide and the hosts for permission before taking photographs, especially in Mixquic and Huaquechula.

## A 9-day culinary tour of Mexico: food and history in one journey

**Discovering Mexican cuisine is woven into the journey from Mexico City to the Caribbean Sea.** Over 9 days and 8 nights, you visit markets, taste street food and mezcal, and then see archaeological sites in central Mexico and on the Yucatán Peninsula. The journey concludes in Cancún, with free days to relax.

This option is for travelers interested in food as part of everyday city life, rather than merely a tasting dinner at a restaurant. Gastronomy features in **several dedicated excursions**, while the remaining days are devoted to landmarks, cenotes and leisure. The trip is not a nine-day cooking course.

Unlike the [8-day Mexico Lindo itinerary](/mexico/tour/mexico-lindo-eight-days/), this tour emphasizes markets, tacos, mezcal and free days on the coast. The [12-day Fantastic Mexico tour](/mexico/tour/fantastic-mexico-tour/) devotes more time to Chiapas, ancient Maya cities and long overland journeys.

## Mexico City: markets, Xochimilco and street food

The first days are spent in the capital. A walk through [Coyoacán](/mexico/place/coyoacan/) is combined with local cuisine, while a visit to [Xochimilco](/mexico/place/xochimilco/) reveals the surviving canals of Mexico City's historic lake landscape. A boat trip and walks through city neighborhoods show very different sides of the capital.

The culinary program includes San Juan and Medellín markets, traditional taquerías and tastings of tacos, quesadillas and mezcal. Corn, chili peppers and mole sauces are especially worth exploring: they appear in many combinations in Mexican cooking, and individual dishes are the best introduction.

**It is important to distinguish tastings from a full all-inclusive meal plan.** The itinerary includes culinary excursions and their specified tastings, while drinks outside those inclusions are listed as additional expenses.

## How gastronomy is combined with archaeology

In central Mexico, a trip to [Teotihuacan](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/) is included. The Pyramids of the Sun and Moon form part of one of Mesoamerica's principal ancient urban complexes. Together with the [historic center of Mexico City](/mexico/place/mexico-city-and-teotihuacan/), this part of the route introduces the legacy of different eras.

After flying to [Cancún](/mexico/place/cancun/), the itinerary explores the Yucatán Peninsula. It includes [Chichén Itzá](/mexico/place/chichen-itza/) and visits to cenotes, followed later by [Cobá](/mexico/place/coba/), [Tulum](/mexico/place/tulum/) and [Gran Cenote](/mexico/place/gran-cenote/). Allow sufficient time to see the Maya sites, as they are spread across different parts of the peninsula.

Chichén Itzá's oldest structures reflect a complex history of influences from different Maya cultures and central Mexico. However, a general Yucatán excursion is not the same as a multi-day archaeological expedition: here, cultural outings alternate with leisure.

## How the nine days are divided

| Part of the journey | Highlights |
|---|---|
| Days 1–3 | Mexico City, markets, Xochimilco, Teotihuacan |
| Days 4–5 | Flight, Chichén Itzá, cenote |
| Days 6–8 | Cancún, Cobá, Tulum, free days |
| Day 9 | Departure transfer |

There are no mandatory excursions on days six and eight in Cancún. You can use this time for the beach or independent leisure. If you prefer a slower pace, consider leaving both free days clear of additional long-distance trips.

The route also crosses different climate zones: from high-altitude Mexico City to the warm Caribbean Sea. Pack comfortable shoes for city walks, sun protection for archaeological sites and swimwear for the cenotes, taking local visiting rules into account.

## What is included and which expenses remain

The package includes 8 hotel nights in the stated category or comparable accommodation, breakfasts, specified tastings, lunch during the Chichén Itzá excursion, transfers and daytime excursions with English- or Spanish-speaking assistance. **The inclusion of a Russian-speaking guide on every excursion has not been confirmed.**

Exclusions specifically include the **Mexico City–Cancún flight**, other air tickets, taxes and fees, beverages not listed as included, tips and personal expenses. The terms also mention separate local charges in the state of Quintana Roo; check the final amount against the applicable rules before traveling.

When choosing a trip, it is useful to compare both [other Mexico tours](/mexico/tour/) and [food and wine journeys](/interests/food-and-wine/). On some itineraries, cuisine shapes the entire journey; here it complements a cultural tour and a Caribbean getaway.

## Frequently asked questions about the Mexico culinary journey

### Is the whole tour devoted to food and tastings?

No. The dedicated culinary days take place in Mexico City, while other excursions cover Teotihuacan, Chichén Itzá, Cobá, Tulum and the cenotes.

### Are all drinks included in the price?

No. Only the drinks and tastings explicitly listed in the program are included. Others are paid for separately.

### Can I enjoy the beach in Cancún?

Yes. The itinerary includes free days in Cancún, alternating with sightseeing excursions around Yucatán.

### Do I need to purchase the Mexico City–Cancún flight separately?

Yes. This domestic flight is explicitly listed among expenses not included in the package.

## Mexico Lindo in 8 days: from Mexico City via Mérida to the coast

**This cultural itinerary is easy to extend with an independent holiday on the Caribbean Sea.** The program lasts 8 days and 7 nights: 4 nights in [Mexico City](/mexico/place/mexico-city-and-teotihuacan/) and 3 in [Mérida](/mexico/place/merida/). Excursions take in museums, ancient cities, the Xochimilco canals and Yucatán cenotes.

An important detail: the final day ends with a transfer to the Riviera Maya, but **accommodation on the coast is not included in the specified 7 nights**. This makes the tour suitable for travelers who want to explore the sights first and then, if they wish, extend their holiday independently in Cancún, Playa del Carmen or Tulum.

This differs from the [nine-day culinary tour](/mexico/tour/mexico-gourmet-discovery-2024/), which already includes overnight stays and free days in Cancún.

## Why spend four nights in Mexico City?

The first part of the trip introduces the capital's history. The itinerary includes the historic center, the National Museum of Anthropology, [Teotihuacan](/mexico/place/teotihuacan/) and the Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe. Another excursion explores the canals of [Xochimilco](/mexico/place/xochimilco/), where the traditional waterways of Mexico City's ancient lake basin survive.

Four nights in the city make it possible to spread out the sightseeing days without changing hotels daily. There are, however, scheduling restrictions: under the program's conditions, the National Museum of Anthropology is not visited on Mondays, while the Xochimilco excursion operates **on Wednesdays, Fridays and Sundays**. Coordinate these days while selecting your departure dates.

## Mérida, Uxmal and cenotes: another chapter of Mexican history

After the flight from Mexico City, you begin exploring [Mérida](/mexico/place/merida/) and the Yucatán Peninsula. Day five is devoted to the flight and a walk through the city's historic center. On day six, you visit [Uxmal](/mexico/place/uxmal/) and [Kabah](/mexico/place/kabah/), Maya sites known for the distinctive stone architecture of the Puuc region.

The next excursion takes you to the [Santa Bárbara cenotes](/mexico/place/santa-barbara-cenotes/). The listed inclusions include cenote admission, a life jacket and travel between the sites by bicycle or horse-drawn carriage. Swimming in cenotes differs from swimming at an open-sea beach: follow the rules of each individual site.

The final sightseeing day features [Chichén Itzá](/mexico/place/chichen-itza/), a stop in [Valladolid](/mexico/place/valladolid/) and a transfer to the [Riviera Maya](/mexico/place/riviera-maya/). This is a full cultural sightseeing day, so it should not be treated as a full leisure day at a resort hotel.

The tour's **2027 rates** depend on room occupancy: TPL — **5219 USD**, DBL — **5336 USD**, SGL — **5870 USD** per person. These rates correspond to different numbers of guests sharing a room, so it would be misleading to compare them as a single price without specifying occupancy.

Included are 7 nights in the two cities, the listed transfers and excursions with bilingual English- and Spanish-speaking assistance, and admission to the named attractions. A Yucatecan-style lunch is provided on the final day.

Paid separately are the **Mexico City–Mérida flight**, other meals and drinks, tips, personal expenses and **a hotel for any extension on the Caribbean coast**. Transfers to certain hotel areas in Tulum and Bahía Petempich are also excluded, so arrange your exact drop-off location in advance.

## Who will find this itinerary convenient?

The program suits lovers of history, architecture and archaeology who want to see two regions of Mexico without constantly changing hotels. Days involve substantial walking at monuments and trips outside the cities, but there is no requirement to follow a major expedition route through the jungles of Chiapas.

If you would like to add a beach holiday, Ada Tours can help arrange it as a separate extension. **The eight days of the main itinerary should not be presented as a beach holiday with a coastal hotel included.**

For more options, explore the [Mexico tours](/mexico/tour/) and the themed [culture and history journeys](/interests/culture-and-history/).

## Frequently asked questions about Mexico Lindo

### Is a hotel on the Riviera Maya included?

No. The package includes 4 nights in Mexico City and 3 in Mérida. Accommodation after reaching the Caribbean coast is chosen separately.

### Is the domestic flight to Mérida included?

No. The Mexico City–Mérida flight is paid for separately, although airport transfers specified in the itinerary are included.

### What languages are the excursions conducted in?

English and Spanish. These rates do not confirm the inclusion of Russian-speaking assistance.

### Can I choose any dates for the museum and Xochimilco?

The days need to be coordinated with the schedule. When planning, account for the Anthropology Museum being closed on Mondays and Xochimilco excursions operating on Wednesdays, Fridays and Sundays.
